---
title: "Part 2 - immunogenetr and the matching API"
---

# immunogenetr is an R package for the day-to-day work of an HLA lab: cleaning up typing, turning it into GL strings, and counting matches and mismatches. It is on CRAN, so it installs like any other package, and every function has a help page with examples.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(immunogenetr)
library(httr2)
```

# Typing usually comes out of a lab information system as a table, with one column per allele. HLA_typing_LIS is an example. 

```{r}
HLA_typing_LIS
```

# HLA_columns_to_GLstring() turns those columns into a single GL string per person: alleles at one locus are joined by "+", and loci are joined by "^".

```{r}
(LIS_GL <- HLA_typing_LIS |>
  mutate(
    GL_string = HLA_columns_to_GLstring(
      pick(everything()),
      HLA_typing_columns = mA1Cd.recipient:mDPB12cd.recipient,
      prefix_to_remove = "m",
      suffix_to_remove = "Cd.recipient"
    )
  ) |>
  select(patient, GL_string))
```

# Patient 3 needs a stem cell transplant. Let's rank everyone else in the table as a potential donor by the classic "out of 10" match grade (A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1).

```{r}
patient_GL <- LIS_GL |>
  filter(patient == 3) |>
  pull(GL_string)

LIS_GL |>
  rename(donor = patient) |>
  # Put the patient's typing on every row, next to each donor's typing.
  mutate(patient_GL = patient_GL) |>
  mutate(match_grade = HLA_match_summary_HCT(
    patient_GL,
    GL_string,
    direction = "bidirectional",
    match_grade = "Xof10"
  )) |>
  select(donor, match_grade) |>
  arrange(desc(match_grade))
```

# Patient 3 matches itself 10/10, of course; the others are made-up people. Every donor was scored at once, and the same code would work for ten thousand donors. But there's a catch: immunogenetr compares allele names as written. Here is a recipient and donor who differ only at DRB1: 14:01 versus 14:54.

```{r}
recipient <- "HLA-A*02:01+HLA-A*24:02^HLA-B*07:02+HLA-B*44:02^HLA-C*05:01+HLA-C*07:02^HLA-DRB1*04:01+HLA-DRB1*14:01"
donor     <- "HLA-A*02:01+HLA-A*24:02^HLA-B*07:02+HLA-B*44:02^HLA-C*05:01+HLA-C*07:02^HLA-DRB1*04:01+HLA-DRB1*14:54"

HLA_match_summary_HCT(recipient, donor, direction = "bidirectional", match_grade = "Xof8")
```

# 7/8. But DRB1*14:01 and 14:54 have the same antigen recognition domain: they are in the same P group, so for matching they count as a match. Reducing typing to P groups needs py-ard and the IPD-IMGT/HLA Database, which is more than you want to set up on every computer in the lab.

# So the same matching runs as a free web service: the immunogenetr matching API (https://api.immunogenetr.org). We send it the two GL strings, it reduces them to P groups with py-ard, matches them with immunogenetr, and sends back the answer.

```{r}
request("https://api.immunogenetr.org/match/hct") |>
  req_body_json(list(
    gl_string_recip = recipient,
    gl_string_donor = donor,
    match_grade = "Xof8",
    preprocess = TRUE   # reduce to P groups first
  )) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json() |>
  str()
```

# 10/10, and the answer records exactly which database and software versions produced it. Because it's a web service, anything can use it, not just R. For example, https://hct-report.immunogenetr.org builds a one-page donor match report on top of this API, with no coding at all.
